learner_capabilities.success_statement: Recognize a sequential-choice problem in which later legal choices depend on earlier selections.
Explain in words why legal sequential choice counts multiply.
Reconstruct nPr from the shrinking sequence n, n-1, ..., n-r+1 instead of recalling it as an isolated formula.
Distinguish without-replacement ordered selection from repeated-choice and unordered-selection models.
Select and execute the counting model when the slots are disguised as roles or constrained positions.

concept_anchor.description: Fill three distinct labelled roles from a pool without reusing a person; show the legal choice count shrinking after each assignment.
concept_anchor.learner_job: Predict the number of legal choices for the next slot before multiplying anything.

learning_units.ordinary_language_target: For an ordered sequence of choices, count the legal options for each next step and multiply those step counts; when reuse is forbidden, the available pool shrinks.

term_origins: n is the number of legal choices for the first ordered slot.
Each subsequent factor decreases by one because an already used object cannot be selected again.
There are r factors because exactly r ordered slots are filled.
The factorial quotient is a compression of the same finite product, not a new counting rule.
conditions: The r positions or selections are ordered or otherwise distinguishable.
An object cannot be reused unless the problem explicitly permits repetition.
0 <= r <= n for the without-replacement nPr form.
formal_understanding.reconstruction_route: Draw r ordered slots, write the number of legal choices above each slot, multiply the shrinking counts, then compress the product into factorial notation.
checks: For r=1 the count reduces to n.
For r=n the count becomes n!.
Changing only the names of the slots must not change the count.

representation_transitions.learner_job: Translate each slot into the number of choices still legal at that stage.
Compress the shrinking product without losing the meaning of its factors.

misconceptions.wrong_model: Use n choices at every ordered position even when selections cannot be repeated.
misconceptions.why_tempting: The first slot has n choices, so repeating the same visible count for all later slots looks superficially symmetric.
misconceptions.decisive_discriminator: Ask whether an object selected earlier remains legal for the next slot; if not, the choice count must shrink.

contrasts.case_a: Choose a president and secretary from five students.
contrasts.case_b: Choose two students to form an unlabeled pair from five students.
contrasts.decisive_difference: In case A, swapping the two students changes who holds each role; in case B, the same two-person set is unchanged.

completion_probes.prompt_intent: Hide nPr and ask the learner to rebuild the count for r ordered slots from the shrinking legal choices.
completion_probes.success_evidence: The learner states why each factor appears and gives the condition under which the factors shrink.

completion_probes.prompt_intent: Contrast an ordered role-assignment problem with an unordered pair-selection problem and ask why the counts differ.
completion_probes.success_evidence: The learner identifies order/role identity as the decisive modelling difference rather than selecting a formula by keyword.

completion_probes.prompt_intent: Use a constrained seating or code-position problem where the ordered slots are not named as permutations and require the learner to choose the model.
completion_probes.success_evidence: The learner identifies the legal-choice sequence, handles the new constraint, and justifies the multiplication before simplifying.

recognition_requirements: Determine whether earlier choices remove later legal choices.
Separate the model-selection step from arithmetic execution.
failure_models: Use a constant n choices at every stage.
Treat an ordered role assignment as an unordered selection.
